questions.a: High TSH with low free T4
d: High TSH with normal free T4
Low TSH with low free T4
Low TSH with high free T4
questions.why: High TSH with a normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism. Low TSH with low free T4 points to the pituitary, and low TSH with high T4 is hyperthyroidism.

questions.q: What is the usual full replacement dose of levothyroxine?
questions.a: About 1.6 micrograms per kg per day
d: About 0.5 micrograms per kg per day
About 3 micrograms per kg per day
About 5 micrograms per kg per day
options: About 0.5 micrograms per kg per day

About 3 micrograms per kg per day
About 5 micrograms per kg per day
questions.why: Older patients and those with coronary disease start at 25 to 50 micrograms and titrate, because a sudden full dose can provoke angina or arrhythmia.

questions.q: After a levothyroxine dose change, when should TSH be rechecked?
questions.why: TSH lags because levothyroxine's half-life is about a week and the pituitary takes several half-lives to settle. Checking earlier gives a misleading number.

questions.q: Which should be separated from levothyroxine by about four hours?
questions.why: Also coffee, soy and fibre. The drug is best taken on an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, or at bedtime a few hours after the last meal.

questions.q: In subclinical hypothyroidism, at what TSH is treatment generally recommended?
questions.why: Between the upper limit of normal and 10, treatment is considered for symptoms, positive antibodies, or pregnancy; otherwise TSH is repeated, since a third normalise on their own.

questions.q: A woman on levothyroxine confirms a pregnancy. What is the immediate dose change?
questions.a: Increase the dose by about 25% to 30% now
d: No change until the first TSH
Stop it for the first trimester
questions.why: Requirement rises from the first weeks, and maternal hypothyroidism affects fetal brain development. Many patients are told to take two extra tablets a week on a positive test.

questions.q: Low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH. What does this suggest, and what is followed during treatment?
questions.why: With a pituitary or hypothalamic cause the TSH cannot be trusted. Adrenal function is checked before starting levothyroxine, since replacing thyroid first can precipitate an adrenal crisis.

questions.q: A hospitalised patient with pneumonia has a mildly low TSH and low T3. What is the right response?
questions.a: Recheck 6 weeks after recovery; do not treat now
questions.why: Non-thyroidal illness distorts every thyroid test. Thyroid function is best not tested during acute illness unless thyroid disease is the suspected cause.
Amiodarone can cause either hypo- or hyperthyroidism through its iodine load. Checkpoint inhibitors cause thyroiditis that often ends in hypothyroidism.

questions.q: A patient taking high-dose biotin has a low TSH and a high free T4 but no symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.why: Biotin interferes with the immunoassays used for thyroid tests, mimicking hyperthyroidism. Stopping it for a few days and repeating the tests resolves the picture.

questions.q: Which antibody confirms Hashimoto thyroiditis as the cause of hypothyroidism?
questions.why: TSH receptor antibodies point to Graves disease. Anti-TPO positivity in subclinical hypothyroidism predicts progression and tips the decision toward treatment.

questions.q: Which harms follow long-term over-replacement with a suppressed TSH?
questions.why: Both are dose related and matter most in older patients, where the target TSH is often relaxed toward the upper half of normal for that reason.
